title: How a water mill turns a river into flour
topic: How a medieval water mill works: the wheel, the axle, the gears and the millstones.

props.describe: a small wooden water mill with a big wooden water wheel on its side, stone base, shingled roof
a pair of round grey stone millstones stacked on top of each other with a wooden spindle through the middle

sources: Reynolds, T. S. (1983). Stronger than a Hundred Men: A History of the Vertical Water Wheel. Johns Hopkins University Press
Domesday Book (1086) records about 5,600 water mills in England

beats.text: Hi hi! This little house can turn a river into bread. No electricity. At all!
beats.title: A RIVER THAT MAKES BREAD

beats.text: It's a water mill, and people used them for over two thousand years. Let me show you how it works!
Step one. The wheel. River water pushes the paddles, and the whole wheel turns. Round and round, all day long.
beats.label: WATER PUSHES PADDLES

beats.text: Water is heavy, so even a slow stream carries a lot of power.
Step two. The axle. The wheel sits on a thick wooden shaft that goes right inside the mill.
beats.label: WHEEL SPINS A SHAFT

beats.text: Inside, wooden gears turn that sideways spin into an upright one, and speed it up.
Step three. The millstones! Two huge round stones. The bottom one stays still, the top one spins.
beats.label: TOP STONE SPINS

beats.text: Pour grain in the middle hole, and it gets crushed between them into flour.
Back in ten eighty six, England's Domesday Book counted over five thousand of these mills!
beats.label: 5,600 MILLS IN 1086

beats.text: River, wheel, gears, stones, bread. Follow for more old tech that still feels like magic!
